text:
In view of the improved air quality and reduced traffic congestion available through the use of mass transit, an airport shuttle service should be considered as an alternative to building at least part of the proposed spur. A shuttle system serving parking facilities for Chicago's O'Hare Field is already under construction. A shuttle plan for Mitchell Field might take the following form, for example.
The high capacity freeway could terminate at the point where it meets the railroad line and transportation the rest of the distance to the airport could be provided by a relatively narrow, at-grade parkway designed for use by an efficient mass transit shuttle service. A commuter depot could be provided at the rail line and automobile parking could be provided at the depot and along the parkway. Parking and shuttle vehicle stops would be arranged to minimize the distance air passengers would have to carry their luggage, and the shuttle vehicle would take them right to the airport terminal building.
With savings in roadway construction costs, more money could be devoted to planting trees along the parkway which would make it more pleasant to use than a freeway with a concrete barrier down the center. Use of the shuttle service could also be encouraged by setting much higher parking fees at the air terminal parking lot than the parkway park-and-ride cost. The availability of shuttle service to the airport at short intervals would, in turn, encourage the development of commuter service on the railroad.
This plan would reduce air pollution along the last mile of travel to the airport because a large number of cars would be replaced by a few mass transit vehicles. Division of parking between the parkway and the air terminal would aid the dispersion of automobile emissions and a reduction rather than an expansion of parking at the terminal might be possible. This would help to avoid some of the complex air pollution problems that can be expected in a large airport parking lot when automobile emissions are combined with aircraft emissions. In addition, the problem of the proposed spur blocking the tower's view of part of one runway would be avoided with a parkway built at-grade.
Local Meteorology
All of the proposed spur sites lie within five miles of the western shore of Lake Michigan in an area where meteorological conditions are influenced by the presence of the lake. Cole and Lyons (1) believe that the environmental impact statement for a project in such an area, in considering impact on air quality, should "include a detailed study of the local air pollution meteorology, including the lake effect." This information is missing from the airport spur draft EIS.
